label: Directional Derivatives And Subgradients
notes: Open by naming the central replacement for a missing gradient. Convexity gives a one-sided directional derivative in every direction, and subgradients turn those one-sided rates into visible supporting hyperplanes for the epigraph. The lecture arc moves from local slope to global affine certificate.

label: One-Sided Slope
notes: Use the secant picture to separate one-sided information from ordinary differentiability. For convex functions, the forward difference quotients settle monotonically as the step length shrinks. The limit can be infinite, but it exists, and as a function of the direction it is convex and positively homogeneous.

label: Epigraph Support Plane
notes: The epigraph view is the geometric heart of the section. A subgradient at x is not merely a local slope; it draws a nonvertical affine hyperplane that touches the epigraph at the boundary point and leaves the whole epigraph on one side.

label: Subgradient Inequality
notes: Present the inequality as a certificate that can be checked against every possible comparison point. Once a candidate vector passes the global inequality, the affine function through the base point is a lower support to the graph, so local visual contact becomes a global guarantee.

label: Subdifferential Set
notes: The subdifferential collects all valid certificates at a point. Because each comparison point contributes a closed halfspace condition in the candidate slope variable, the resulting set is closed and convex. It may be empty, a singleton, an interval, or a higher-dimensional body.

label: Absolute Value Example
notes: The absolute value cusp is the cleanest nonsmooth example. Away from zero the subdifferential is a singleton matching the ordinary derivative. At zero, every slope between minus one and one supports the graph, so the subdifferential is the whole interval.

label: Max Of Affine Functions
notes: For a pointwise maximum of affine functions, inactive pieces sit strictly below the envelope and do not constrain the local support. The active affine pieces determine the kink, and the subdifferential is the convex hull of their slopes.

label: Normal Cone Relation
notes: Indicator functions translate subgradient language into normal cone language. If the function is zero on a convex set and infinite outside it, the subgradient inequality says precisely that the candidate vector forms a nonpositive angle with every feasible displacement.

label: Directional Derivative As Support Function
notes: This slide closes the loop between directional derivatives and subgradients. Under the standard closed proper interior hypotheses, the directional derivative in direction y is obtained by maximizing the linear probe against the subdifferential set. Emphasize the inspection target: the support-function picture turns a possibly one-sided slope into an optimization problem over all supporting hyperplanes at the base point.

label: Optimality
notes: The first-order condition becomes almost literal. If zero is a subgradient at x, then the subgradient inequality reduces to saying every other point has value at least f of x. Conversely, a minimizer makes the zero affine floor valid.

label: Numerical Subgradient Checks
notes: Treat the displayed formulas as executable geometry. The check table samples points, slopes, and directions for the absolute value and max-affine examples. The important residual is the amount by which the graph stays above its proposed affine support.

label: Failure And Smooth Contrast
notes: End the examples by warning that finite value at a point is not the same as subdifferentiability. Interior points of a proper convex domain have subgradients, while certain boundary points can force vertical support behavior and leave no nonvertical affine minorant.

label: Recap
notes: Close with the compressed dictionary. Directional derivatives are one-sided support values, subgradients are affine certificates, subdifferentials are the sets of all certificates, normal cones are indicator subdifferentials, and optimality is detected by the presence of zero.
